title: threading your art into your day
content:
not “making more time for art,” but threading art into time

in an ideal week, I’d be able to wade into my artistic projects for long, uninterrupted swaths of time — and it would feel as luxurious and soul-nourishing as taking a cool swim in a crystal clear bay every morning, before breakfast. (I did this once during a roadtrip last year, it was amazing).

but, the reality I find myself in, more often than not, is continually waiting for the openness of that spacious day… and… I just keep waiting. it never comes on its own. I feel busy with a gazillion other things: growing my digital ecosystem, writing newsletters, making podcasts, teaching courses, doing client work, and I keep waiting, and waiting, while feeling a static guilt in the back of my mind.

I catch myself in all or nothing thinking. as in:

IF I don’t have [X hours] to completely dive in and lose myself in my creative projects, THEN anything less is somehow deeply insufficient.

the lurking shadow thought that comes afterwards, of course, is —

IF I can’t even prioritize my creative work, then I’m not a real artist.

 

beyond the daily creative ritual

for many years, my solution for this was the daily creative ritual. I held myself to a daily creative discipline, every morning —

  1. upon awakening: creative free writing for 15-30 minutes

  2. then — yoga, movement, meditation, breakfast

  3. after breakfast: draw something (in Procreate)

  4. and/or: writing a new entry in this public journal — around any idea I was thinking about, or anything on my mind.

  5. if complete, publish it immediately.


I did this sequence of practices, more or less consistently, for over six years. I changed countries, lives, relationships — and returned to this practice as my inner anchor. the point was the process. my daily consistency gifted me with so much — a deep sense of self-trust, an evolving personal style, a safe container for spontaneity and experimentation. it helped me overcome my perfectionism in sharing my work, and build the 600+ posts in my archives.

but. the same time, I craved something more fluid. I craved the sensation of getting lost in the work, of feeling the gravity of falling inwards. I craved deep dives, or sprint sessions where I could pour more intensity into a singular project, and pull out something more knotty, difficult, and substantive.

I wrote about these two ways of working — rituals vs. sprints, representing two different ways of moving with creative energy.


interweaving creativity into a day

then, this year, I felt my creative body desire something different — beyond the binary of rituals vs. sprints.

I wanted more variety. I wanted to fall inwards from one obsession to another, without feeling the fear or panic that comes with resurfacing to “the real world.” but even more than that — I wanted my practices to feel deeply embedded in the fabric of a day — stitched into the spare moments, rather than overly boundaried in the designated “morning creative time” — and forgotten about the rest of the day.

I wanted my inability to adhere to my blocked calendar times — of long, three hour writing sessions — to not feel like a failure at being an artist/writer. I wanted to make space for those long sessions to come organically, unplanned if they wanted to — like an unexpected loved one who showed up at my house at 10PM on a weeknight. they are the kind of visitor that I’d put away everything for. I’d give them my fullest attention and forget that it was past bedtime.

that’s how I wanted to relate to my art.

touching the thread

okay, how? how do you keep the thread of a creative project alive — in that liminal space between rituals and sprints?

I think that the simple answer is: you touch that thread everyday — multiple times a day, as many times as you can.

there’s many ways of touching a thread. how you engage with its energy is entirely up to you — it could be in the few minutes while waiting for the kettle to boil. it could be a few notes, jotted down, while walking your dog in the park. instead of 10 minutes scrolling on your phone, refreshing your email, reading anxiety-inducing news articles. you could do a 5 minute sketch, a 3 minute meditation on your project. you can spend 1 absent-minded minute to day dream about it.

I’ll be writing in more detail about my specific tools and practices in the next weeks, but here’s a shortlist of my favorite practices for this.

  • micro-sessions as portals — allowing myself 3-4 min, or 7-8 min, or 12 min to tune into the pulse of a project, and jot down a a few notes.

  • daily depositions - this is what I call my practice of inner listening + notetaking in my journal. I attune to what’s stirring in me, and I jot it down.

  • the syllabus as body-web — for bigger projects, I’ve been playing with the form of a self-directed syllabus as guiding the spine of research, independent studies, ongoing micro-session practices, and culminative projects.

  • tangible symbol as anchor - currently I’m starting to work a book project that I’ve been incubating for many, many years. I choose 2 rocks for this project — one to represent the bigger project (the full book), and a smaller rock to represent the first tiny iteration of it.

  • while going on walks - I bring a tiny notebook to jot down ideas that come to me. sometimes the insights that come unlock a new dimension or provide a magic key.

  • while cooking (especially baking) - same as above. I keep my notebook to jot down questions.

  • while taking a shower — super cliche, but true. I’m wondering about working more actively with the element of water.

  • talking to Claude as sounding board - I really need to talk about how I use AI, because this has been one of the most transformative changes of my year. I don’t use Claude to do any sort of creation work, but mostly as a sounding board for my ongoing verbal processing and ideas, and as synthesis.

keeping an ongoing conversation alive

perhaps the most important thing — beyond any specific practices — is the core intention of keeping an ongoing conversation with your creative work alive, outside of any “designated creative blocked time.”

even if you don’t have time for a deep dive / sprint session, or if you feel too impatient/overwhelmed/distracted for a daily consistent rituals — there’s this. love and relationship doesn’t (only) need such boundaried, pre-scheduled time.

if you love something deeply, if you want to center your art as the one and most important thing that feels true, then all you need to do is simple.

keep talking to it.

you’d steal away moments from your busy day to call it, text it, scribble secret love notes, plot escapes and imagine dreams together, or discuss little domestic details, like… what color should your title font be? what do you feel like doing this week? what do you want for dinner (nourishment) this weekend?

your only job, then, can be distilled to simply this —

keep the conversation with your Art alive. you talk to it. you ask it questions. then you listen. you listen to what it wants, and you let it lead your way.
